summary: At just 1.2 square miles with over 22,000 residents packed in at roughly 18,500 people per square mile, Cudahy is one of the most densely populated cities in all of California — denser than San Francisco by some measures — yet it has no high-rise skyline, no subway station, and no downtown district to explain that compression. The city sits on the flat, featureless floor of the Los Angeles Basin, wedged between the 710 freeway corridor and the concrete-channeled Los Angeles River, in a stretch of southeastern L.A. County dominated by warehousing, light manufacturing, and logistics operations that serve the nearby ports. That industrial spine shapes daily life: this is overwhelmingly a commuter city, with most employment tied to the broader regional economy rather than anything within the 1.2-mile footprint. Housing costs reflect a metro-wide squeeze — the median home sits around $505,300 against a median household income of roughly $52,700, yielding a price-to-income ratio near 9.6x, which effectively prices out most local earners from ownership and keeps renting (median $1,667/month) as the default. Mild year-round temperatures averaging 76°F daytime highs and 55°F lows, with over nine hours of daily sunshine, mean the climate is genuinely pleasant — but open green space is scarce relative to the density. Cudahy is, in essence, the math of Southern California's housing pressure made visible on a single square mile of flat ground.
